description: Azizbek leads frontend development, crafting high-performance interfaces and translating complex data into clear, interactive visualizations. Rayyona drives the project's scientific foundation, researching core domain concepts and ensuring technical logic remains accurate and impactful.
summary: Planet X and SPHEREx is a public web tool for spotting motion and brightness changes in NASA’s infrared sky survey. Choose a patch of sky to blink between aligned visits, subtract or stack images, overlay Gaia and AllWISE sources, or extract a spectrum at a selected point. The tool flags possible motion for human review. A spatial index covering more than 1.6 million SPHEREx exposures lets the viewer find observations without waiting for a live archive search. If the server restarts during a comparison, the viewer can rebuild it from the original exposures and keep the selected visits. Students, citizen scientists, and researchers can share a sky patch so others can inspect the same field.
details:
How it works

Choose a sky patch and set the field of view, date range, and wavelength range. The viewer searches a bundled SQLite index of 1,628,230 calibrated SPHEREx Level 2 exposures from DR1 and QR3, then reads the FITS data needed for the patch from NASA/IPAC IRSA’s public cloud archive. A scheduled refresh reads headers for new or changed files and keeps the last validated index available if a refresh fails. We verified that the public deployment could find observations and render real images from both releases with live IRSA metadata search disabled. For matched playback, the viewer checks wavelength and usable coverage, aligns the visits on a common north-up grid, and uses the same display contrast across frames. Deployment verification

From a blink to a closer look

Blink between visits to spot movement or a change in brightness. Subtract two visits to highlight change, or average several aligned visits to bring out faint structure. Pixel flags help identify suspect measurements, while ESA Gaia DR3 and NASA AllWISE overlays show where cataloged sources are expected. Select a point to build a near-infrared spectrum from available observations. Where enough comparable visits exist, the motion search proposes tracks across three or more visits for users to inspect against the original images. These are leads for follow-up; the tool does not confirm discoveries.

The viewer can restore an open Auto or Manual comparison after a server restart, using the same exposures and selected visits when they’re still available. Shared patch links prefill the sky picker, and embedded views start the comparison automatically. On touchscreens, panning and pinch zoom leave the patch selection in place.

We checked the motion search on known movers, including WISE 0855 and Epsilon Indi B. In a held-out two-visit test, the detector recovered 31 of 128 injected movers. The results help users decide which candidates to inspect in the original images and follow up with additional visits.

We also ran a four-field pilot using the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube to test whether combining wavelength channels within a detector improves point-source sensitivity. In 20 measurable detector and field combinations, the composites reached a median of 0.83× the signal-to-noise of the strongest individual channel. That result informed our proposed Bands browser, with individual channels as the default and detector composites as an optional broadband view. Bands proposal and pilot results

Why we built it

Blink comparison helped astronomers discover Pluto. We brought the same technique to current SPHEREx data and connected it to the checks a volunteer needs when something looks unusual. Users can share a link or embed the selected patch and filters so someone else can repeat the inspection. Matching wavelength, checking overlapping coverage, and showing pixel flags reduce the chance of mistaking differences between observations for a moving source. Reading only the data needed for a patch keeps the interaction practical without requiring a full detector download in the browser.

Tools and AI disclosure

The interface uses TypeScript, React, Vite, and CDS Aladin Lite. The Python API uses FastAPI, Astropy for FITS and sky coordinates, NumPy and SciPy for image and numerical processing, and Pillow for image output. OpenAI Codex assisted with coding, debugging, and drafting this submission text. The survey images and catalog measurements come from the credited archives.

Source code and setup instructions are available in the sac26 GitHub repository.
